az sql db create -g $rg -s $server -n $db -e GeneralPurpose --compute-model Serverless \
  -f Gen5 --min-capacity 0.5 -c 2 --auto-pause-delay 60     # -c = max vCores
# Hyperscale serverless: -e Hyperscale (minimum auto-pause delay 60)
CREATE DATABASE testdb  ( EDITION = 'GeneralPurpose', SERVICE_OBJECTIVE = 'GP_S_Gen5_1' );
CREATE DATABASE testdb2 ( EDITION = 'Hyperscale',     SERVICE_OBJECTIVE = 'HS_S_Gen5_2' );
Auto-pause: prevented by geo-replication (active geo-replication and failover groups), LTR, a DNS alias on the logical server, the sync database of SQL Data Sync and a job database of elastic jobs. It resumes with a login (the first attempt returns error 40613, “database unavailable”: retry) or when viewing/modifying Query Store, recommendations, auditing or TDE. Latency ≈ 1 min (resume) and 1–10 min (pause): use retry logic. The free offer is GP serverless (up to 10 DBs per subscription, 100,000 vCore-seconds + 32 GB of data and 32 GB of backup per month, no SLA).

Elastic pools

  • For many DBs with low average and infrequent, non-simultaneous spikes; with just 2 S3 DBs there may already be savings. DBs with persistent medium-high load should not share a pool.
  • Pool size: MAX(N DBs × average usage per DB, DBs with concurrent peak × peak usage per DB) (DTU or vCores) and, in addition, the total storage.
  • No per-DB charge: billed every hour at the maximum of eDTUs/vCores. An eDTU costs 1.5× the individual DTU; in vCore, the price per vCore is the same as for a single DB. Min/max per DB configurable. Hyperscale elastic pools: GA.

Zone redundancy and read scale-out

TopicDetails
Zone redundancyvCore: GP (provisioned and serverless), BC and Hyperscale. DTU: Premium only (Basic and Standard no). DC-series: no. In BC/Premium at no extra cost (it relocates its replicas to other zones).
Read scale-outPremium/BC: 1 free read replica, enabled by default. Hyperscale: HA replicas (0–4) + named replicas (up to 30). Basic/Standard/GP: none; use geo-replica or failover group.
Replica connectionConnection string with ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly (default ReadWrite). Verify with DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'Updateability') → READ_ONLY.
ConsistencyAsynchronous propagation (tens of ms to seconds, no fixed bound). On read replicas, transactions always use SNAPSHOT.
Exam: heavy reporting that degrades OLTP without changing tier → ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly on BC/Premium/Hyperscale (GP has no read scale-out). Many SaaS DBs with staggered spikes → elastic pool. Development DB with sporadic use → serverless with auto-pause.

Compatibility level, IQP and database scoped configurations Azure SQL DB SQL Server 2016+ SQL database in Fabric

The compatibility level determines the behavior of the optimizer/CE and which IQP features are available. Microsoft never raises it automatically.

SELECT name, compatibility_level FROM sys.databases WHERE name = DB_NAME();
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET COMPATIBILITY_LEVEL = 170;
PlatformDefault in new DBsSupported levels
Azure SQL DB / Fabric170170, 160, 150, 140, 130, 120, 110, 100
SQL Server 2016 → 2025130 (2016) · 140 (2017) · 150 (2019) · 160 (2022) · 170 (2025)Up to its own level (2025 supports 100–170)
Managed Instance170 (Always-up-to-date or SQL Server 2025 policy) · 160 (SQL Server 2022 policy; watch out: the doc table lists 150 and the text 160)—
Minimum levelIQP features (Azure SQL DB)Notes
No level requirementApproximate COUNT DISTINCT · Memory grant feedback percentile and persistence (active in all DBs) · Optimized plan forcing · OPTIMIZED_SP_EXECUTESQLAPPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT. Persistence requires Query Store READ_WRITE (SQL Server 2022: level ≥ 140). Scoped configs: OPTIMIZED_PLAN_FORCING ON, OPTIMIZED_SP_EXECUTESQL OFF (avoids compilation storms; SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL DB, Fabric)
110Approximate percentileSQL Server 2022+; APPROX_PERCENTILE_CONT/DISC
140Batch mode adaptive joins · Interleaved execution (MSTVF) · Batch mode memory grant feedbackAdaptive join chooses nested loops or hash at runtime
150Batch mode on rowstore · Row mode memory grant feedback · Scalar UDF inlining · Table variable deferred compilationInlining rewrites the scalar UDF as a relational expression
160Parameter Sensitive Plan (PSP) optimization · CE feedback · DOP feedbackCE and DOP feedback require Query Store READ_WRITE. DOP_FEEDBACK: OFF by default in SQL Server 2022 (you must enable it with DOP_FEEDBACK = ON); ON by default in SQL Server 2025; Azure SQL DB: GA since Jul 2025 (default not documented → Verify in sys.database_scoped_configurations)
170Optional parameter plan optimization (OPPO) · CE feedback for expressionsOPPO: several plans for @p IS NULL OR … predicates
  1. Capture a baseline in Query Store at the current level.
  2. Raise the level in a test environment (ALTER DATABASE … SET COMPATIBILITY_LEVEL) and rerun the workload.
  3. Compare with Regressed Queries; if there are regressions, force the previous plan with sp_query_store_force_plan while you investigate.
  4. Targeted adjustments: hint QUERY_OPTIMIZER_COMPATIBILITY_LEVEL_n / FORCE_LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION (via USE HINT or Query Store hints) or LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION = ON.
Watch out: a DB created with an earlier default, or imported from a BACPAC / restored, keeps its level (e.g. 160) until you change it. Since level 130, optimizer fixes and CE changes only reach the latest default level.
Exam: PSP → level 160; OPPO → 170; batch mode on rowstore and scalar UDF inlining → 150. Raising the level safely = Query Store (baseline) + plan forcing, not changing it blindly in production.

Database scoped configurations (MAXDOP and others)

Engine settings per database, without changing tier. Permission: ALTER ANY DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION (whoever has CONTROL on the DB can grant it).

ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP = 4;
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION FOR SECONDARY SET MAXDOP = 1;   -- replicas (PRIMARY = inherit)
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION = ON;
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET PARAMETER_SNIFFING = OFF;
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET QUERY_OPTIMIZER_HOTFIXES = ON;
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS = ON;
ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION CLEAR PROCEDURE_CACHE;   -- accepts <plan_handle>

SELECT name, value, value_for_secondary FROM sys.database_scoped_configurations;
OptionDefaultEquivalent / notes
MAXDOP0 (uses the server config) · 8 on new Azure SQL DB and Fabric DBs (single and elastic pool)Priority: hint OPTION (MAXDOP n) > scoped (if ≠ 0) > sp_configure; cap per Resource Governor workload group. It is a limit per task
LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATIONOFF (CE according to compat level)ON = trace flag 9481; per query: USE HINT('FORCE_LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION')
PARAMETER_SNIFFINGONOFF = TF 4136; per query: OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN or USE HINT('DISABLE_PARAMETER_SNIFFING')
QUERY_OPTIMIZER_HOTFIXESOFFON = TF 4199; per query: USE HINT('ENABLE_QUERY_OPTIMIZER_HOTFIXES')
OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADSOFFStores a compiled plan stub on the 1st execution and the full plan on the 2nd → less plan cache bloat from single-use queries
PARAMETER_SENSITIVE_PLAN_OPTIMIZATIONON from level 160PSP: multiple plans per parameterized query
OPTIONAL_PARAMETER_OPTIMIZATIONON from level 170OPPO
CE_FEEDBACK · DOP_FEEDBACKCE_FEEDBACK ON from level 160 · DOP_FEEDBACK OFF (SQL Server 2022) / ON (SQL Server 2025)They require Query Store in READ_WRITE. DOP_FEEDBACK: OFF in SQL Server 2022 (DOP feedback page: “not enabled by default in SQL Server 2022”); ON in SQL Server 2025 (“What's new in SQL Server 2025”: “Now on by default” and the Microsoft blog “Smarter Parallelism”); in Azure SQL DB it is GA since Jul 2025 (Azure SQL DB “What's new”) with no default indicated. The ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION reference still says “The default is OFF” with no version → Verify the actual value in sys.database_scoped_configurations. Query hints to disable them per query: DISABLE_DOP_FEEDBACK · DISABLE_CE_FEEDBACK
LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATSOFFEnables sys.dm_exec_query_plan_stats (last actual plan)
ASYNC_STATS_UPDATE_WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITYOFFWith async auto-update: the update waits for the Sch-M lock in a low-priority queue
PREVIEW_FEATURESOFFEnables features in Preview; not for production
MAXDOP in Azure SQL DB: default 8 since Sep 2020 for new DBs (earlier ones do not change). 0 = min(logical processors, 64): Microsoft recommends avoiding MAXDOP 0 (an analytic query can exhaust CPU and threads). A MAXDOP in CREATE/ALTER INDEX overrides the DB-level one only for that operation; the scoped MAXDOP also governs DBCC CHECKDB.
Watch out: with FOR SECONDARY, all secondaries share the same configuration (each one is not set individually). It runs on the primary and by default the secondaries inherit (PRIMARY).
Exam: an analytical query consumes all the threads and degrades checkout → keep MAXDOP 8 (or lower) and use the per-query hint; a different read workload on the replica → FOR SECONDARY; plan cache full of single-use plans → OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS.

Automatic tuning and index recommendations Azure SQL DB Fabric SQL Server 2017+ (FLGP only)

Managed service that monitors queries, applies fixes and validates them: if there is no improvement (or there is a regression) it reverts them by itself. It acts only during periods of low CPU, Data IO and Log IO utilization and needs Query Store active in READ_WRITE.

OptionWhat it doesDefault (Azure defaults)Availability
FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLANDetects plan regression and forces the last good plan (automatic plan correction)ONSQL DB, Managed Instance, Fabric (and SQL Server 2017+)
CREATE_INDEXCreates recommended indexes and verifies the improvementOFF (in Fabric it is enabled automatically)SQL DB single/pooled and Fabric; no in MI
DROP_INDEXDrops unused indexes (last 90 days) and duplicatesOFFSQL DB single/pooled; no in MI
 
-- INHERIT: inherits from the server (individual options in DEFAULT)
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING = INHERIT;
-- AUTO: Azure defaults
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING = AUTO;
-- CUSTOM: each option accepts ON | OFF | DEFAULT
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING (CREATE_INDEX = ON, DROP_INDEX = ON);
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING (FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN = ON);

SELECT * FROM sys.database_automatic_tuning_options;     -- status (e.g. "Disabled by the system")
SELECT * FROM sys.dm_db_tuning_recommendations;          -- recommendations and their status
  • Validation of each change: from 30 minutes to 72 hours depending on execution frequency; on any regression it is reverted immediately.
  • CREATE_INDEX: does not recommend if the index would take the space used to > 90% of the max data size, nor for tables whose clustered index/heap is > 10 GB; once creation has started it is not paused.
  • DROP_INDEX: never drops unique indexes (PK/UNIQUE); it disables itself if there are queries with index hints or partition switching; in Premium and BC it drops only duplicates (not the unused ones).
  • Recommendations applied manually with T-SQL: without automatic validation or rollback; they stay listed for 24–48 h. Change history: 21 days.
  • Database Advisor (portal): viewing recommendations = Reader / SQL DB Contributor; executing actions = Owner / SQL DB Contributor.
Exam: the recommended way with many DBs is to configure it on the server and use INHERIT on the DBs. Leave FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN ON (it catches overnight regressions) and CREATE_INDEX/DROP_INDEX OFF until you review what they propose.
Watch out: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN = ON fails if Query Store is not enabled and in READ_WRITE. With INHERIT, the three individual options must be set to DEFAULT. Plans forced by the service show up with plan_forcing_type = AUTO in sys.query_store_plan.
Sources: Learn · Recommend database configurations · Docs · Automatic tuning · Docs · Performance recommendations

Transaction isolation levels: locking vs row versioning SQL Server Azure SQL DB GA

They define how much a transaction sees of the uncommitted work of other transactions. The 4 classic levels use pessimistic concurrency (locks); RCSI and SNAPSHOT use optimistic (row versioning). Writing always takes an X lock until the end of the transaction, regardless of the level.

LevelDirty readNon-repeatablePhantomReaders ↔ writersMechanism
READ UNCOMMITTEDYesYesYesDo not block each otherNo S locks (= NOLOCK)
READ COMMITTED (locking)NoYesYesBlock each otherShort S locks. Default SQL Server (RCSI OFF)
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI)NoYesYesDo not block each otherSnapshot per statement. Default Azure SQL DB
REPEATABLE READNoNoYesBlock each otherS locks until the end of the transaction
SNAPSHOTNoNoNoDo not block each otherSnapshot per transaction; possible update conflicts
SERIALIZABLENoNoNoBlock each otherKey-range locks until the end of the transaction (= HOLDLOCK)
 
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL
    { READ UNCOMMITTED | READ COMMITTED | REPEATABLE READ | SNAPSHOT | SERIALIZABLE };

ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;  -- RCSI (SQL Server)
-- Azure SQL DB: this ALTER (RCSI) is run connected to master and with the DB name:
-- ALTER DATABASE [MiBD] SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON;                         -- allows SNAPSHOT

SELECT name, is_read_committed_snapshot_on, snapshot_isolation_state_desc
FROM sys.databases WHERE name = DB_NAME();
DBCC USEROPTIONS;   -- session isolation level
CriterionRCSISNAPSHOT
DB optionREAD_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOTALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION
How to request itREAD COMMITTED level (default); does not change the codeSET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT before starting the transaction
Version it readsCommitted at the start of each statementCommitted at the start of the transaction
Update conflictsNo detection; with optimized locking they retry on their ownBuilt-in detection (cannot be turned off): error 3960, the transaction is aborted → the app must retry
Default Azure SQL DB / SQL Server · Managed InstanceON / OFF · OFFON / OFF · OFF
  • Only one level at a time; it lasts for the whole connection. Inside an SP/trigger it is reset on exit; UDFs cannot run it. A table hint overrides it for that table (READCOMMITTEDLOCK forces locks even if RCSI is ON).
  • Switching to SNAPSHOT from another level inside an already started transaction aborts it; switching from SNAPSHOT to another level is allowed.
  • READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT requires that there be no other active connections (single-user is not needed); ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION waits for active transactions to finish. RCSI cannot be enabled on master, tempdb or msdb.
  • Learn mentions “six levels”: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL accepts only 5 (RCSI = READ COMMITTED + DB option).

Version store: tempdb vs PVS (ADR)

  • With ADR the versions live in the persistent version store (PVS) of the DB itself; without ADR, in the tempdb version store.
  • ADR is always on in Azure SQL DB / MI / Fabric (it cannot be turned off). SQL Server 2019+: ALTER DATABASE … SET ACCELERATED_DATABASE_RECOVERY = ON (PERSISTENT_VERSION_STORE_FILEGROUP = …). It gives constant-time recovery, instantaneous rollback and aggressive log truncation.
  • Cost: more log and page splits in write workloads; the PVS consumes your DB storage. If it fills up: with ADR, DML statements that need to generate versions can fail (“ADR might fail to generate versions, causing DML statements to fail”); with the tempdb version store, writes keep running without generating versions (notice 3959) and transactions that need those versions fail (error 3958).
  • Monitor with sys.dm_tran_persistent_version_store_stats (persistent_version_store_size_kb = off-row versions only). It grows due to long-running transactions/snapshots and a high abort rate (sys.dm_tran_aborted_transactions).
Exam: readers blocking writers without touching code → RCSI (already ON in Azure SQL DB). Several queries with consistent results within a transaction, without blocking → SNAPSHOT. Avoid phantoms (double booking, reconciliation) → SERIALIZABLE or UPDLOCK + HOLDLOCK, accepting more blocking and deadlocks.
Learn vs docs: Learn says that for SNAPSHOT “you must enable ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION”; according to the locking and row versioning guide, in Azure SQL DB it is already ON (OFF by default in SQL Server and in Managed Instance, where you do have to enable it; check it in sys.databases.snapshot_isolation_state_desc). At any level: transactions as short as possible.
Sources: Learn · Preserve data integrity with isolation levels · Docs · SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL · Docs · Locking and row versioning guide · Docs · Accelerated database recovery

Locks: modes, compatibility, escalation, hints and optimized locking SQL Server Azure SQL DB

ModeUse / key fact
Shared (S)Reads; released when the read finishes, except under REPEATABLE READ or higher / hint
Update (U)Before updating; only one U per resource (compatible with S); it converts to X. Also with UPDLOCK
Exclusive (X)INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; incompatible with everything
Intent (IS, IX, SIX…)Table → page → row hierarchy: they signal that lower-level locks will exist (also IU, SIU, UIX); the engine only checks them at table level
Schema (Sch-S, Sch-M)Sch-S when compiling/executing (does not block transactional locks); Sch-M on DDL and TRUNCATE (blocks everything)
Bulk update (BU)BULK INSERT / OPENROWSET(BULK) with TABLOCK (or table lock on bulk load)
Key-rangeSERIALIZABLE; prevents phantoms (RangeS-S, RangeS-U, RangeI-N, RangeX-X…)

Lockable resources: RID, KEY, PAGE (8 KB), EXTENT (8 pages), HoBT, TABLE, FILE, APPLICATION, METADATA, ALLOCATION_UNIT, DATABASE and XACT (lock on the TID with optimized locking).

Requested ↓ / Granted →ISSUIXSIXX
ISYesYesYesYesYesNo
SYesYesYesNoNoNo
UYesYesNoNoNoNo
IXYesNoNoYesNoNo
SIXYesNoNoNoNoNo
XNoNoNoNoNoNo

Lock escalation

AspectValue
TriggerA statement acquires ≥ 5,000 locks on a single table/index reference (it does not add up different indexes or two references of a self-join); the engine checks it every 1,250 new locks. Also if lock memory exceeds 24% of the engine's memory (locks = 0) or 40% of the locks value
TargetRow/key → table directly (never to page). Partitioned table with LOCK_ESCALATION = AUTO → partition (HoBT)
ControlTable option LOCK_ESCALATION: TABLE (default) · AUTO · DISABLE (prevents most escalations, not all)
 
ALTER TABLE dbo.T SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = { AUTO | TABLE | DISABLE });

Locking and timeout table hints

HintEffectNotes
NOLOCK / READUNCOMMITTEDDirty reads; no S locksMay read uncommitted or inconsistent data
READCOMMITTEDLOCKS locks even if RCSI is ONDisables RCSI for that table
REPEATABLEREADREPEATABLE READ semantics on that table—
SERIALIZABLE / HOLDLOCKSERIALIZABLE semantics: key-range locks until the end of the transactionThey are equivalent
UPDLOCKU locks until the end of the transactionThe “SELECT with UPDLOCK and then UPDATE” pattern avoids the S → X conversion deadlock
XLOCKX locks until the end of the transaction—
ROWLOCK · PAGLOCK · TABLOCK(X)Force the lock granularityTABLOCKX = exclusive table lock
READPASTSkips locked rows (row locks, not page locks)Only READ COMMITTED / REPEATABLE READ; with RCSI ON and READ COMMITTED it requires READCOMMITTEDLOCK
NOWAITImmediate error if there is a lock= SET LOCK_TIMEOUT 0 for that table; does not work with TABLOCK
 
-- ms; -1 = wait forever (default); 0 = do not wait
SET LOCK_TIMEOUT 1800;
SELECT @@LOCK_TIMEOUT;
Error 1222 (“Lock request time out period exceeded”): the statement is canceled but the transaction is not rolled back (except with SET XACT_ABORT ON) → catch the error and issue an explicit ROLLBACK. CREATE/ALTER/DROP DATABASE ignore LOCK_TIMEOUT.

Optimized locking

  • TID locking: a single X lock on the transaction ID instead of many row/page locks; those are released as soon as each row is modified. LAQ (lock after qualification): evaluates the predicate on the latest committed version without a lock and only locks the rows that qualify; requires RCSI.
  • Requires ADR. Azure SQL DB, Fabric and Managed Instance (Always-up-to-date / SQL Server 2025 policy): always on. SQL Server 2025: off by default; enabled per DB (requires ADR) with ALTER DATABASE … SET OPTIMIZED_LOCKING = ON | OFF. SQL Server 2022 and earlier: does not exist.
  • Verify: SELECT DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'IsOptimizedLockingOn'); → 1 / 0 / NULL (not available). Less lock memory, fewer escalations and fewer deadlocks; does not affect schema locks. Avoid locking hints: they reduce its benefit.
Exam: mass updates that end up locking the entire table → escalation (≥ 5,000 locks): split into batches, better indexes, LOCK_ESCALATION or optimized locking. In Azure SQL DB (RCSI + optimized locking) readers do not block and write locks are released per row.
Sources: Learn · Isolation levels and optimized locking · Docs · Locking guide · Docs · Optimized locking · Docs · Table hints · Docs · SET LOCK_TIMEOUT

Concurrency controls: pessimistic and optimistic patterns, app locks and retry SQL Server Azure SQL DB

The Learn case (two customers read StockCount = 1 and both buy) is solved with a concurrency technique, not by raising the isolation level of the whole DB.

TechniqueTypeWhenCost
Atomic UPDATE with predicate—Deduct stock / reserveMinimal
UPDLOCK when readingPessimisticRead → decide → writeBlocks other writers
UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCKPessimistic (range lock)“If it does not exist, insert” (double booking)Key-range locks
rowversionOptimisticLong edit with few conflictsRetry if the row changed
SNAPSHOTOptimisticConsistent reads within the transactionVersion store; conflict → 3960
sp_getapplockApplication lockSerialize a logical process (job, import)Depends on the lock
 
-- 1) Atomic UPDATE: no window between read and write
UPDATE dbo.Products SET StockCount = StockCount - @Qty
WHERE ProductID = @ProductID AND StockCount >= @Qty;
IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 THROW 50001, 'Insufficient stock', 1;

-- 2) Read with UPDLOCK and then write
DECLARE @Stock int;
BEGIN TRAN;
SELECT @Stock = StockCount FROM dbo.Products WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) WHERE ProductID = @ProductID;
IF @Stock >= @Qty
    UPDATE dbo.Products SET StockCount = StockCount - @Qty WHERE ProductID = @ProductID;
COMMIT;

-- 3) “Insert if not exists” without phantoms or conversion deadlock
BEGIN TRAN;
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Reservations WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK)
               WHERE RoomID = @RoomID AND SlotDate = @SlotDate)
    INSERT dbo.Reservations (RoomID, SlotDate) VALUES (@RoomID, @SlotDate);
COMMIT;
-- Column: RowVer rowversion NOT NULL (8 bytes, changes on every UPDATE of the row)
UPDATE dbo.Products SET Price = @NewPrice
WHERE ProductID = @ProductID AND RowVer = @OriginalRowVer;
IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 THROW 50002, 'Another user modified the row', 1;

-- Transaction-level app lock
BEGIN TRAN;
DECLARE @r int;
EXEC @r = sp_getapplock @Resource = N'Job:NightlyImport', @LockMode = 'Exclusive',
                        @LockOwner = 'Transaction', @LockTimeout = 0;
IF @r < 0 BEGIN ROLLBACK; RETURN; END    -- < 0 = the lock was not obtained (see table)
-- ... exclusive work ...
COMMIT;                                      -- releases the lock (owner = Transaction)
SET XACT_ABORT ON;
DECLARE @try int = 0;
WHILE @try < 3
BEGIN
    BEGIN TRY
        BEGIN TRAN;
        -- ... DML ...
        COMMIT;
        BREAK;
    END TRY
    BEGIN CATCH
        IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK;
        -- retryable: deadlock, update conflict (SNAPSHOT), lock timeout
        IF ERROR_NUMBER() IN (1205, 3960, 1222) AND @try < 2
        BEGIN
            SET @try += 1;
            WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01';                          -- in production: random delay
        END
        ELSE THROW;
    END CATCH
END;
Data pointValue
sp_getapplock · @LockModeShared, Update, IntentShared, IntentExclusive, Exclusive
sp_getapplock · @LockOwnerTransaction (default; must run inside a transaction) or Session
sp_getapplock · return value0 granted · 1 granted after waiting · -1 timeout · -2 canceled · -3 deadlock victim · -999 parameter error
Retryable errors1205 deadlock victim · 3960 update conflict (SNAPSHOT) · 1222 lock timeout
XACT_ABORT ON: any run-time error rolls back the whole transaction (it avoids transactions left open after timeouts or cancellations and the blocking they leave behind). Trade-off: statements after the error are not executed.
Watch out: after error 1205 the engine has already rolled back the victim transaction; an unconditional ROLLBACK in the CATCH (as in the Learn example) can fail with error 3903. Check XACT_STATE() or @@TRANCOUNT. Error 1222, by contrast, does not roll anything back (with XACT_ABORT OFF, the default).
Retries: randomize the wait (e.g. 1–3 s) so the same two transactions do not collide again, and keep transactions short (no waiting for user input or external calls inside the transaction).
Sources: Learn · Isolation levels · Learn · Blocking and deadlocks · Docs · sp_getapplock · Docs · SET XACT_ABORT

Execution plans: estimated vs actual, operators and warnings SQL Server Azure SQL DB

I want…HowNotes
Estimated plan (does not execute)SET SHOWPLAN_XML ON · SSMS Display Estimated Execution Plan (Ctrl+L)Operators and estimated rows based on statistics
Actual plan (executes)SET STATISTICS XML ON · SSMS Include Actual Execution Plan (Ctrl+M)Adds actual rows, timings, memory grants and warnings. With “Include Actual Execution Plan” enabled, the SET does not return the XML
Live progressSSMS Include Live Query StatisticsUses sys.dm_exec_query_profiles; can slow down the query; permissions SHOWPLAN (DB) + VIEW SERVER STATE (SQL Server) or VIEW DATABASE STATE (Azure SQL DB Premium; on Standard/Basic: server admin or Microsoft Entra admin)
Plan in cachesys.dm_exec_query_plan(plan_handle)Cached plan (no actual metrics)
Last actual plan in cachesys.dm_exec_query_plan_stats(plan_handle)Requires LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS = ON (OFF by default)
Historical plansQuery Store (sys.query_store_plan.query_plan and SSMS reports)Several plans per query and comparison between them
I/O and CPU of a querySET STATISTICS IO ON · SET STATISTICS TIME ONIO: scan count, logical reads (8 KB pages from cache), physical reads, read-ahead and lob reads. TIME: parse/compile times and CPU/elapsed in ms
Permissions: SHOWPLAN on each referenced DB + permission to run the query (SET STATISTICS TIME does not require SHOWPLAN). Live Query Statistics is an SSMS feature intended for diagnostics (it can slow down the query).
Learn vs docs: Learn says plans are read “left to right, top to bottom” and that the first operators access the base tables. The official documentation says right to left and top to bottom (arrow direction = data flow): the leaf operators that read the tables are on the right and the SELECT (root) is on the left. At run time the root “pulls” the data (pull-based); the operators reference adds that both reading directions are useful (right→left: what data enters each operator; left→right: which operator drives the work).
Operator / signalWhat it indicatesTypical action
Index SeekKey-directed access (efficient)Ideal; check residual predicates
Index / Table ScanIndex Scan, Clustered Index Scan or Table Scan: reads all rows (or a wide range)An index is missing or the predicate is not sargable. Not always bad (small table or it returns almost everything)
Key / RID LookupKey Lookup (clustered) or RID Lookup (heap): for each row it goes back to the base table for columns the index does not coverAdd those columns with INCLUDE; watch out for the size and the write cost
Nested LoopsFor each outer row it searches the inner inputGood with a small outer input and an indexed inner input
Merge JoinJoins two inputs sorted by the keyEfficient if they already arrive sorted; otherwise a Sort appears
Hash MatchBuilds an in-memory hash table (build / probe)Large unsorted inputs; needs a memory grant and can spill
SortSorts in memory (or tempdb)An index that already provides the order avoids it
SpoolStores intermediate rows in tempdbInvestigate the source (e.g. correlated subqueries)
ParallelismGather / Repartition / Distribute Streams: parallel plan (yellow arrows)Waits CXPACKET/CXCONSUMER; check MAXDOP
Estimated ≠ actualThick arrows: too many rows pass through early, or a wrong estimateFilter earlier, index, UPDATE STATISTICS; suspect parameter sniffing
Missing Index (green text)The optimizer thinks an index would reduce the costRight-click → Missing Index Details…; review before creating
Warning (yellow triangle)CauseSolution
Missing statisticsNo statistics on a column; the optimizer guessesCreate/update statistics
Excessive memory grantRow overestimation; wasted memoryUpdate statistics, filter earlier
No Join PredicateCartesian productReview the ON clause
Implicit conversionCONVERT_IMPLICIT: different types (e.g. nvarchar parameter vs varchar column); the column is converted and the seek becomes a scanMatch the parameter and column types
Sort / Hash spillThe granted memory was not enough (underestimation) and it spilled to tempdbUPDATE STATISTICS or reduce rows before the sort
 
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderHistory_CustomerDate
ON dbo.OrderHistory (CustomerID, OrderDate DESC)
INCLUDE (ProductID, Quantity, UnitPrice, Status);
Exam: Key Lookup that dominates the cost → add included columns to the nonclustered index. Clustered Index Scan due to a highly selective filter → nonclustered index on those columns. Estimated rows ≪ actual → stale statistics. Always compare estimated vs actual rows in the actual plan.

Performance DMVs: what each one is for and typical queries SQL Server Azure SQL DB

DMV / DMFPurposeKey columns
sys.dm_exec_requestsRequests running right nowstatus, command, wait_type, wait_time (ms), blocking_session_id, cpu_time, logical_reads, open_transaction_count, percent_complete, transaction_isolation_level (1 RU · 2 RC · 3 RR · 4 SER · 5 SNAP)

sys.resource_statsHistory in master: 5 min averages for 14 days—
sys.dm_user_db_resource_governanceActual resource limits of the DB—
 
SELECT TOP 10
    qs.total_worker_time / qs.execution_count AS avg_cpu_time_us,
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_logical_reads / qs.execution_count AS avg_logical_reads,
    SUBSTRING(st.text, (qs.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
        ((CASE qs.statement_end_offset WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(st.text)
          ELSE qs.statement_end_offset END - qs.statement_start_offset) / 2) + 1) AS query_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats AS qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) AS st
ORDER BY avg_cpu_time_us DESC;
SELECT r.session_id, r.status, r.command, r.wait_type, r.wait_time, r.blocking_session_id,
       r.cpu_time, r.logical_reads, t.text AS query_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id AND s.is_user_process = 1
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
ORDER BY r.cpu_time DESC;

SELECT TOP 10 wait_type, waiting_tasks_count, wait_time_ms, signal_wait_time_ms
FROM sys.dm_db_wait_stats          -- in SQL Server: sys.dm_os_wait_stats
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
SELECT wt.session_id, wt.wait_duration_ms, wt.wait_type, wt.blocking_session_id,
       tl.resource_type, tl.request_mode, tl.request_status
FROM sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks AS wt
JOIN sys.dm_tran_locks AS tl ON tl.lock_owner_address = wt.resource_address;

SELECT TOP 20 end_time, avg_cpu_percent, avg_data_io_percent, avg_log_write_percent
FROM sys.dm_db_resource_stats ORDER BY end_time DESC;       -- one row every 15 s

SELECT OBJECT_NAME(s.object_id) AS tbl, i.name AS idx,
       s.user_seeks, s.user_scans, s.user_lookups, s.user_updates
FROM sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats AS s
JOIN sys.indexes AS i ON i.object_id = s.object_id AND i.index_id = s.index_id
WHERE s.database_id = DB_ID() AND s.user_seeks + s.user_scans + s.user_lookups = 0;
Wait typeMeaning
LCK_M_*Waiting for a lock (LCK_M_S Shared, LCK_M_U Update, LCK_M_X Exclusive, LCK_M_IX Intent Exclusive…) → blocking
PAGEIOLATCH_SHWaiting for I/O of a data page (slow disk or excessive reads)
WRITELOGWaiting for the log flush (commits, checkpoints)
CXPACKET · CXCONSUMERSynchronization of a parallel plan; CXCONSUMER is normal
SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELDA task yields the scheduler and waits for its quantum (CPU pressure)
RESOURCE_SEMAPHOREQuery waiting for its memory grant
THREADPOOLNo worker available (worker limit)
ASYNC_NETWORK_IOThe client does not consume the results fast enough
Permissions: Azure SQL DB → VIEW DATABASE STATE (or VIEW DATABASE PERFORMANCE STATE); on Basic/S0/S1 and elastic pool DBs: server admin, Microsoft Entra admin or the ##MS_ServerStateReader## server role (##MS_ServerPerformanceStateReader## for the new performance DMVs). SQL Server ≤ 2019 and MI: VIEW SERVER STATE; SQL Server 2022+: VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE.
Exam: DMVs = volatile current or cumulative state (lost when the plan is evicted from the cache or on restart); Query Store = persistent history. Strategy: DMVs to locate the expensive queries → execution plan to find out why. Always look at execution_count together with the average cost.

Query Store: enable and configure (ALTER DATABASE … SET QUERY_STORE) Azure SQL DB SQL Server 2016+ Fabric

Captures text, plans and statistics inside the DB in 3 stores: plan store, runtime stats store (aggregated per interval) and wait stats store (per query and plan). Writes asynchronously. Captures only DML (not DDL) and cannot be enabled on master or tempdb.

ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE = ON (OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE);

ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE (
    OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
    CLEANUP_POLICY = (STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30),
    DATA_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 900,
    MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 1024,
    INTERVAL_LENGTH_MINUTES = 60,
    SIZE_BASED_CLEANUP_MODE = AUTO,
    QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO,
    MAX_PLANS_PER_QUERY = 200,
    WAIT_STATS_CAPTURE_MODE = ON
);
-- deletes the data (CLEAR ALL: last resort if the state is ERROR)
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE CLEAR;
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE (
    QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = CUSTOM,
    QUERY_CAPTURE_POLICY = (
        STALE_CAPTURE_POLICY_THRESHOLD = 24 HOURS,
        EXECUTION_COUNT = 30,
        TOTAL_COMPILE_CPU_TIME_MS = 1000,
        TOTAL_EXECUTION_CPU_TIME_MS = 100));

MAX_PLANS_PER_QUERYnumber; 0 = no limit200200
WAIT_STATS_CAPTURE_MODEON · OFFONON (from 2017)
QUERY_CAPTURE_POLICY (CUSTOM)STALE_CAPTURE_POLICY_THRESHOLD · EXECUTION_COUNT · TOTAL_COMPILE_CPU_TIME_MS · TOTAL_EXECUTION_CPU_TIME_MSDefaults: 1-day window (1 h–7 days) · 30 executions · 1000 ms of compile CPU · 100 ms of execution CPU
 
SELECT actual_state_desc, desired_state_desc, readonly_reason,
       current_storage_size_mb, max_storage_size_mb
FROM sys.database_query_store_options;
-- READ_ONLY with desired READ_WRITE = it switched itself to read-only. Fix:
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET QUERY_STORE (MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 1024);
readonly_reason (bitmap)Cause
1 · 2 · 4 · 8Read-only DB · single-user · emergency · secondary replica
65536MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB was reached (the typical cause)
131072Too many distinct statements (internal memory limit): clean up queries or move up a tier
262144In-memory items pending persistence exceeded the limit (temporary)
524288The DB reached its disk limit
  • It goes back to READ_WRITE only when there is space (raise the maximum or clean up). ERROR state: sp_query_store_consistency_check (SQL Server 2017+; with Query Store disabled) and, if that is not enough, QUERY_STORE CLEAR ALL. sp_query_store_flush_db forces the flush to disk.
  • Best practices: SIZE_BASED_CLEANUP_MODE = AUTO, AUTO capture (or CUSTOM), short retention and parameterize (forced parameterization) to avoid generating thousands of ad hoc queries. Change objects with ALTER, not DROP/CREATE: a recreated object generates new query_id values and the history and forcing are lost.
Discrepancies: the Learn lab says that QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = ALL records short calls to stored procedures that AUTO “might skip”; the docs state that cursors, queries inside stored procedures and natively compiled queries are always captured with ALL, AUTO or CUSTOM. In addition, the SQL Server pages disagree on the capture default since 2019: ALTER DATABASE SET options says AUTO (ALL only in 2016–2017), but sys.database_query_store_options says “ALL by default in SQL Server 2016 and later” and AUTO only for Azure SQL DB; check it in sys.database_query_store_options.
Exam: in Azure SQL DB, Query Store is ON by default, with AUTO capture, and is a prerequisite for QPI, FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN, CE/DOP feedback. If it stays in READ_ONLY because of space, QPI stops showing new data → increase MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB (max. 10 GB) or clean up.
Sources: Learn · Query Store and QPI · Docs · ALTER DATABASE SET options · Docs · Best practices Query Store · Docs · sys.database_query_store_options

Query Store: reports, catalog views, plan forcing and Query Store hints Azure SQL DB SQL Server 2016+ / hints 2022+ Fabric

SSMS reportUse it for…
Regressed QueriesQueries whose performance got worse (plan change). Review it after each deployment, statistics update or index change
Overall Resource ConsumptionTotal DB consumption by metric (daytime/nighttime patterns)
Top Resource Consuming QueriesStarting point for tuning: most expensive queries by metric and interval
Queries With Forced PlansList of forced plans
Queries With High VariationHighly variable performance (usually parameter sensitivity)
Query Wait StatisticsWaits by category (CPU, Lock, Buffer IO, Memory…) and which queries cause them; requires WAIT_STATS_CAPTURE_MODE = ON
Tracked QueriesFollow critical queries in real time (e.g. with a forced plan)

Metrics: Duration (default), CPU Time, Logical/Physical Reads, Logical Writes, CLR Time, DOP, Memory Consumption, Row Count, Log Memory Used, Temp DB Memory Used, Wait Time; aggregation avg / max / min / std dev / total. Catalog views: sys.query_store_query_text, query_store_query, query_store_plan, query_store_runtime_stats, query_store_runtime_stats_interval, query_store_wait_stats, query_store_query_hints, query_store_plan_feedback, query_store_query_variant (PSP) and sys.database_query_store_options.

SELECT q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
FROM sys.query_store_query_text AS qt
JOIN sys.query_store_query AS q ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
WHERE qt.query_sql_text LIKE N'%GetCustomerOrders%' AND qt.query_sql_text NOT LIKE N'%query_store%';

SELECT p.plan_id, p.is_forced_plan, p.force_failure_count,
       SUM(rs.count_executions) AS execs,
       SUM(rs.avg_duration * rs.count_executions)
           / NULLIF(SUM(rs.count_executions), 0) AS avg_duration_us
FROM sys.query_store_plan AS p
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
WHERE p.query_id = 42
GROUP BY p.plan_id, p.is_forced_plan, p.force_failure_count
ORDER BY avg_duration_us;
    EXEC sp_query_store_force_plan   @query_id = 42, @plan_id = 17;   -- optional: @disable_optimized_plan_forcing (bit, default 0), @replica_group_id
    EXEC sp_query_store_unforce_plan @query_id = 42, @plan_id = 17;   -- optional: @replica_group_id

EXEC sys.sp_query_store_set_hints @query_id = 42,
     @query_hints = N'OPTION (MAXDOP 1, MAX_GRANT_PERCENT = 10)';
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_set_hints @query_id = 42, @query_hints = N'OPTION (RECOMPILE)';
-- inside the string, single quotes are doubled
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_set_hints @query_id = 42,
     @query_hints = N'OPTION (USE HINT (''FORCE_LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION''))';
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_clear_hints @query_id = 42;
SELECT query_id, query_hint_text, last_query_hint_failure_reason_desc, source_desc
FROM sys.query_store_query_hints;

Plan forcing

  • Immediate fix after a regression, without touching the code; “performance rollback”.
  • Permission: ALTER on the DB.
  • Not guaranteed: if the plan is no longer viable (index or schema changed, online index build) the query compiles normally, the query_store_plan_forcing_failed XEvent fires and force_failure_count goes up (last_force_failure_reason_desc).
  • plan_forcing_type: MANUAL (you) or AUTO (automatic tuning).

Query Store hints

  • They inject hints without changing the query; they persist across restarts and failovers; they override statement hints and plan guides; the latest value replaces the previous one.
  • ALTER permission. SQL Server 2022+, Azure SQL DB/MI, Fabric.
  • Supported: {HASH|ORDER} GROUP, {CONCAT|HASH|MERGE} UNION, {LOOP|MERGE|HASH} JOIN, EXPAND VIEWS, FAST n, FORCE ORDER, KEEP PLAN, KEEPFIXED PLAN, MAX_GRANT_PERCENT, MIN_GRANT_PERCENT, MAXDOP, NO_PERFORMANCE_SPOOL, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, PARAMETERIZATION {SIMPLE|FORCED}, RECOMPILE, ROBUST PLAN, USE HINT…
  • Not supported: OPTIMIZE FOR (@v = val), MAXRECURSION, USE PLAN (use plan forcing), DISABLE_DEFERRED_COMPILATION_TV, DISABLE_TSQL_SCALAR_UDF_INLINING, table hints; nor statements with simple parameterization.
  • If a hint would prevent generating the plan, all are ignored and the reason is recorded in sys.query_store_query_hints.
Preview: Query Store for readable secondaries (SQL Server 2025, Azure SQL DB; always on in SQL DB/Fabric): ALTER DATABASE [db] FOR SECONDARY SET QUERY_STORE = ON (OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE);. Per-replica hints use @replica_group_id; QPI does not yet distinguish replicas.
Exam: “the SP was fast yesterday and is slow today” → Regressed Queries / Top Resource Consuming → compare plans → sp_query_store_force_plan. “Limit parallelism or force RECOMPILE on a query without changing the app” → Query Store hint (sys.sp_query_store_set_hints).
Sources: Learn · Query Store and QPI · Docs · Query Store hints · Docs · sys.sp_query_store_set_hints · Docs · Monitoring with Query Store · Docs · Query Store for secondary replicas

Query Performance Insight (QPI) and which tool to use Azure SQL DB database watcher: Preview, retires Apr 30, 2027

QPI is a portal view over Query Store data: top queries by CPU, duration and number of executions, without SSMS. Only single and pooled databases in Azure SQL Database (not Managed Instance).

AspectDetails
PathPortal → DB → Intelligent Performance → Query Performance Insight
Default viewTop 5 queries by CPU; the top line = DTU % of the DB (maximum per hour; only a high-level comparison); the bars = CPU % per query
Custom tabMetric: CPU · Duration · Execution count; interval: 24 h · week · month; no. of queries: 5 / 10 / 20; aggregation: Sum · Max · Min · Avg
Query details3 charts: CPU, duration and no. of executions over time; Database Advisor annotations (create index, parameterize queries…) that can be applied from the portal
RequirementsQuery Store active (ON by default) and ~a couple of hours of data. RBAC: view charts = Reader, Owner, Contributor, SQL DB Contributor or SQL Server Contributor; view the query text = Owner, Contributor, SQL DB Contributor or SQL Server Contributor
LimitsOnly shows the top 5–20 (many small queries do not appear); does not capture DDL and may omit some ad hoc ones; with Query Store in READ_ONLY there is no new data; a read-only lock on the resource prevents opening the details
ToolUse it when…
Query Performance InsightYou want to see in the portal which queries used the most CPU/time yesterday or last week
Query Store (Regressed Queries)A query got worse after a deployment or plan change → compare plans and force the good one
Query Store (Query Wait Statistics)You need the waits attributed to each query (WAIT_STATS_CAPTURE_MODE = ON)
Request and wait DMVsWhat is running and what is blocked right now (sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks)
Actual execution planYou want to know why a specific query is slow (+ STATISTICS IO/TIME)
Missing index DMVs / AdvisorSeveral queries are missing indexes (Database Advisor, automatic tuning CREATE_INDEX)
Metrics and dm_db_resource_statsCheck whether the DB is at the limit of its tier (DTU / CPU %)
Deadlocks alertNotify of deadlocks (Azure Monitor signal) and analyze them with Extended Events
Database watcher PreviewAdvanced monitoring of the entire fleet (SQL DB and MI), but the docs announce its retirement on Apr 30, 2027 without reaching GA (since Nov 9, 2026 watchers can no longer be created or edited); the replacement is Database Hub in Microsoft Fabric
Exam: QPI depends on Query Store; if the scenario mentions “top consuming queries in the portal without SSMS” it is QPI. For deeper analysis (queries that QPI does not show) use Query Store/SSMS (or Database Hub in Fabric; database watcher is being retired).
Sources: Learn · Query Store and QPI · Docs · Query Performance Insight · Docs · Monitoring and performance tuning · Docs · Database watcher

Missing indexes, index usage, fragmentation and statistics SQL Server Azure SQL DB

sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups joins index_group_handle with index_handle; sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats provides user_seeks, user_scans, avg_total_user_cost and avg_user_impact; sys.dm_db_missing_index_details gives statement, equality_columns, inequality_columns and included_columns.

SELECT TOP 10 mid.statement AS table_name,
       mid.equality_columns, mid.inequality_columns, mid.included_columns,
       ROUND(migs.avg_total_user_cost * migs.avg_user_impact
             * (migs.user_seeks + migs.user_scans), 2) AS improvement_measure
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups AS mig
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats AS migs ON migs.group_handle = mig.index_group_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_details AS mid ON mig.index_handle = mid.index_handle
ORDER BY improvement_measure DESC;
  • Only suggests nonclustered, rowstore, non-unique and non-filtered indexes; calculated from single-query estimates before running it; not for trivial plans either; maximum of 600 groups; it is cleared by a restart, failover, DB offline or a change to the table metadata.
  • It does not order the key columns: equality before inequality and, among equalities, the most selective first. The INCLUDE order does not matter. Combine similar suggestions, review existing indexes (duplicates) and check that the table is not a heap “by accident”.
  • They are recommendations, not commands: test reads and writes. In Azure SQL DB, automatic tuning CREATE_INDEX and Database Advisor validate the result; manually created indexes are not validated.
  • sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats: user_seeks, user_scans, user_lookups, user_updates (counts operations, not rows). Many updates and few reads = candidate to drop; it resets when the service starts or when the DB is detached/shut down.
avg_fragmentation_in_percent (classic rule)Action
< 5 %Nothing (the benefit is not worth it)
> 5 % y ≤ 30 %ALTER INDEX … REORGANIZE — always online; does not update statistics
> 30 %ALTER INDEX … REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) — recalculates statistics (full scan except for a partitioned index or a resumable rebuild)
5% / 30% thresholds: they are the classic heuristic (earlier docs and much of the literature); the current Reorganize and rebuild indexes doc no longer sets thresholds: decide by workload and cost (not only by a fixed fragmentation level) and also look at the page density; UPDATE STATISTICS often gives the same benefit as a REBUILD at much lower cost.
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(ips.object_id) AS tbl, i.name AS idx,
       ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent, ips.page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') AS ips
JOIN sys.indexes AS i ON i.object_id = ips.object_id AND i.index_id = ips.index_id
WHERE ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 5
  AND ips.page_count > 1000;   -- ignores small indexes

ALTER INDEX IX_OrderHistory_CustomerDate ON dbo.OrderHistory REORGANIZE;
ALTER INDEX IX_OrderHistory_CustomerDate ON dbo.OrderHistory REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON);

Statistics

Option / factValue
AUTO_CREATE_STATISTICSON: creates single-column statistics (_WA_Sys_*) on predicate columns
AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICSON: they are updated at compile/execution time if there were enough modifications
AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNCOFF (synchronous). With ON the query does not wait; ASYNC_STATS_UPDATE_WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY avoids blocking others with the Sch-M lock
Modification threshold≤ 500 rows: every 500 changes · > 500 rows: 500 + 20% of n · compat ≥ 130: MIN(500 + 20 % × n, SQRT(1000 × n)) (2 M rows → 44,721 modifications)
ManualUPDATE STATISTICS (default sampling, or WITH FULLSCAN) · sp_updatestats (the whole DB)
 
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.OrderHistory;                 -- default sampling
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.OrderHistory WITH FULLSCAN;
EXEC sp_updatestats;                                -- all tables in the DB
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC ON;
Exam: estimated rows ≪ actual rows in the plan → stale statistics (UPDATE STATISTICS, auto-update). Fragmentation 5–30% → REORGANIZE; > 30% → REBUILD with ONLINE = ON to maintain availability (classic rule).
Sources: Learn · Evaluate query performance · Docs · Missing index suggestions · Docs · Reorganize and rebuild indexes · Docs · Statistics

Parameter sniffing and plan regressions SQL Server Azure SQL DB

The optimizer compiles with the parameter values of the first execution and caches the plan. With skewed data (one customer with 50,000 rows and the rest with < 100) a single plan (seek + lookups vs scan) does not suit all values: “fast yesterday, slow today” after the cache is recycled.

RemedySyntaxNotes
Force the good plansp_query_store_force_planWithout touching code; immediate and temporary fix (may harm other values)
Query Store hintsys.sp_query_store_set_hints with RECOMPILE or OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWNWithout touching code; OPTIMIZE FOR (@p = value) is not supported as a QS hint
RecompileOPTION (RECOMPILE) · WITH RECOMPILE in the proc · sp_recompileTailored plan each time; costs CPU
Do not use the sniffed valueOPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN · USE HINT('DISABLE_PARAMETER_SNIFFING') · OPTIMIZE FOR (@p = value)Uses the average density (or the chosen value)
Global per DBScoped config PARAMETER_SNIFFING = OFF= TF 4136; affects all queries
PSP optimizationCompat ≥ 160 (automatic)Dispatcher plan + query variants based on 3 cardinality ranges per predicate (low/medium/high); only equality predicates; evaluates up to 3 predicates per query (compat 160: only the most skewed one per table reference; compat 170 / SQL Server 2025: several from the same table, one per column, max. 3, and DML/tempdb support). It is disabled with the scoped config PARAMETER_SENSITIVE_PLAN_OPTIMIZATION = OFF or with the query hint DISABLE_PARAMETER_SENSITIVE_PLAN (name given by the PSP doc and a Microsoft support article; usual syntax OPTION (USE HINT('DISABLE_PARAMETER_SENSITIVE_PLAN')), as the OPPO doc confirms for its sibling hint; the USE HINT list in the query hints doc does not include it —nor DISABLE_DOP_FEEDBACK / DISABLE_CE_FEEDBACK— and points to sys.dm_exec_valid_use_hints; some blogs cite …_OPTIMIZATION, with no support in the docs → Verify: SELECT name FROM sys.dm_exec_valid_use_hints WHERE name LIKE 'DISABLE_PARAMETER%'). It is also nullified if sniffing is disabled (TF 4136, PARAMETER_SNIFFING = OFF or DISABLE_PARAMETER_SNIFFING)
Cover the index / statisticsINCLUDE (…) · UPDATE STATISTICSA covering index removes the seek+lookup vs scan decision

Detect: in Query Store, a query with ≥ 2 plans and very different durations (Top Resource Consuming, Regressed, High Variation); in the plan, compare the compiled and runtime parameter values.

  1. Lab: index without INCLUDE and skewed data (CustomerID 1 with 50,000+ rows).
  2. ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION CLEAR PROCEDURE_CACHE; and run the proc with CustomerID 29485 (< 100 rows, GO 10) → the good plan is cached: Index Seek.
  3. Repeat the CLEAR PROCEDURE_CACHE and run it with CustomerID 1 → the Clustered Index Scan is cached.
  4. Run again with CustomerID 29485 (GO 10): it reuses the scan = regression.
  5. EXEC sp_query_store_flush_db; → Top Resource Consuming Queries (Duration · Total · Last hour) → two plans → Force Plan for the Index Seek.
  6. Verify is_forced_plan = 1 and force_failure_count = 0 in sys.query_store_plan.
Exam: “the same stored procedure is fast with some parameters and slow with others” → parameter sniffing. Solution without changing the application → plan forcing or Query Store hint (RECOMPILE); long term: indexes, statistics or rewriting.
Sources: Learn · Exercise: Optimize query performance · Lab · Optimize query performance · Docs · Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization · Docs · Troubleshoot: regression after a version upgrade · Docs · Query hints

Blocking: find the head blocker and resolve it Azure SQL DB Fabric SQL Server

A session requests a lock that is incompatible with another session's lock and waits. A few milliseconds is normal. With RCSI (default in Azure SQL DB) readers do not block writers: typical blocking is writer ↔ writer or caused by stricter isolation levels/hints.

  1. Identify the head blocker: a session with blocking_session_id = 0 that appears as the blocking_session_id of others.
  2. Find out which query/transaction holds the locks (long query? sleeping with an open transaction?).
  3. Analyze the cause (plan, indexes, long transaction, isolation, hints) and resolve it by redesigning the query or the transaction.
  4. KILL only for orphaned/abandoned sessions.
SELECT r.session_id AS blocked_session, r.blocking_session_id,
       r.wait_type, r.wait_time AS wait_ms, r.wait_resource, t.text AS blocked_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Investigate the head blocker (e.g. session 52)
SELECT s.session_id, s.status, s.open_transaction_count, s.login_name, s.host_name, s.program_name,
       s.last_request_start_time, ib.event_info AS last_batch
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_input_buffer(s.session_id, NULL) AS ib
WHERE s.session_id = 52;

KILL 52;                      -- KILL 52 WITH STATUSONLY = rollback progress
SELECT tst.session_id, DB_NAME(tdt.database_id) AS database_name,
       tdt.database_transaction_begin_time, est.text AS last_sql
FROM sys.dm_tran_database_transactions AS tdt
JOIN sys.dm_tran_session_transactions AS tst ON tst.transaction_id = tdt.transaction_id
JOIN sys.dm_exec_connections AS ec ON ec.session_id = tst.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(ec.most_recent_sql_handle) AS est;
Scenariostatus · open_tranDoes it resolve itself?What to do
Long query that is progressingrunnable · ≥ 0Yes, when it finishesOptimize (indexes, fewer rows); SNAPSHOT for reads; move reports to a replica
Sleeping + open txnsleeping · > 0NoIdle session with a transaction without commit/rollback: KILL; in the app, ROLLBACK in error handling and SET XACT_ABORT ON (typical after a timeout or cancellation)
Client does not read all the rows— · ≥ 0No, until it reads or closesFix the app (full fetch); RCSI mitigates it
Session in rollbackrollback · > 0YesWait; avoid bulk loads at peak hours (ADR makes rollbacks fast)
Orphaned connectionsleeping · > 0EventuallyKILL
Data pointValue
Special blocking_session_id values0/NULL not blocked · -2 orphaned distributed transaction · -3 deferred recovery · -4 latch owner not determined (internal transition) · -5 latch owner not tracked (e.g. SH latch): asynchronous wait, does not indicate a problem by itself
wait_resourceTAB: db:objid:idx · PAGE: db:file:page · KEY: db:hobt_id (hash) · RID: db:file:page:slot
Typical waitLCK_M_X = waiting for an exclusive lock (another writer); LCK_M_S/U/IX depending on the mode
KILL permissionSQL Server: ALTER ANY CONNECTION (sysadmin/processadmin) · Azure SQL DB: KILL DATABASE CONNECTION (held by the server-level login). It does not terminate system processes
  • Short transactions with no user interaction inside; SET XACT_ABORT ON; IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK in the app's error handler; read all the rows of the result.
  • Always access objects in the same order; indexes that reduce the rows touched; RCSI/SNAPSHOT; avoid UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK, TABLOCK, READCOMMITTEDLOCK, REPEATABLEREAD unless they are essential.
  • Temporary patch: disabling connection pooling makes releasing the connection roll back open transactions.
Exam: a sleeping session with open_transaction_count > 0 that blocks others = abandoned transaction → identify with sys.dm_exec_requests/sessions and KILL; prevention: short transactions, XACT_ABORT ON, ROLLBACK in the error handler.
Details: Learn filters with session_id > 50 to exclude system sessions (old heuristic); sys.dm_exec_sessions.is_user_process = 1 is more reliable. To trace activity use Extended Events (there is no SQL Profiler in Azure SQL DB).
Sources: Learn · Identify and resolve blocking and deadlocks · Docs · Understand and resolve blocking in Azure SQL DB · Docs · KILL

Deadlocks: detection, capture, prevention and retry Azure SQL DB SQL Server

Cyclic dependency: each transaction holds a lock that the other needs. The deadlock monitor looks for cycles every 5 s (drops to 100 ms if deadlocks are frequent), picks a victim, rolls it back and returns error 1205: “Transaction (Process ID N) was deadlocked on lock resources with another process and has been chosen as the deadlock victim. Rerun the transaction.”

TopicDetails
Victim selection1) lowest DEADLOCK_PRIORITY; 2) the cheapest to roll back (fewest log bytes, “Log Used”); 3) at random. A task that is already rolling back cannot be a victim
SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITYLOW (−5) · NORMAL (0, default) · HIGH (5) · integer from −10 to 10 · variable; set at runtime. It does not prevent the deadlock: it only changes who becomes the victim
Resources in deadlockLocks, worker threads, memory, parallel execution resources (exchange) and MARS
Deadlock graphvictim-list (victim; in SSMS an oval with an X) · process-list (session+transaction: spid, priority, logused, isolation level, waitresource, inputbuf, host/login) · resource-list (resources and who owns or waits for them). It is saved as .xdl
PlatformHow to capture the deadlock graph
Azure SQL DB / FabricCreate an Extended Events session ON DATABASE with sqlserver.database_xml_deadlock_report (ring buffer or event file)
SQL Server / Managed InstanceThe system_health session (active by default) captures xml_deadlock_report; trace flags 1204/1222 write to the error log (avoid them under heavy workloads)
AlertsAzure Monitor → Deadlocks signal (emitted when the deadlock has already been resolved)
 
CREATE EVENT SESSION [deadlocks] ON DATABASE
ADD EVENT sqlserver.database_xml_deadlock_report
ADD TARGET package0.ring_buffer
WITH (STARTUP_STATE = ON, MAX_MEMORY = 4 MB);
GO
ALTER EVENT SESSION [deadlocks] ON DATABASE STATE = START;
GO
WITH ring_buffer AS (
    SELECT CAST(t.target_data AS xml) AS rb
    FROM sys.dm_xe_database_sessions AS s
    JOIN sys.dm_xe_database_session_targets AS t
      ON CAST(t.event_session_address AS binary(8)) = CAST(s.address AS binary(8))
    WHERE s.name = N'deadlocks' AND t.target_name = N'ring_buffer'),
dx AS (
    SELECT x.evt.query('.') AS d
    FROM ring_buffer
    CROSS APPLY rb.nodes(
        '/RingBufferTarget/event[@name=''database_xml_deadlock_report'']') AS x(evt))
SELECT d.value('(/event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS deadlock_time,
       d.query('/event/data[@name=''xml_report'']/value/deadlock') AS deadlock_xml
FROM dx
ORDER BY deadlock_time DESC;
TargetAdvantagesLimitations
ring_bufferT-SQL only; quick to set upDeleted when the session stops or on a failover; uses DB resources; for tests or short term
event_filePersists in an Azure Storage blob; it is downloaded and analyzed without consuming DB resourcesRequires container + SAS (read/write/list) + CREATE MASTER KEY + CREATE DATABASE SCOPED CREDENTIAL; target package0.event_file with filename = 'https://…/deadlocks.xel'

Prevent (from lowest to highest risk)

  • Tune nonclustered indexes (lowest risk, does not touch code): fewer rows read = fewer locks. Check that the table has a clustered index, index the FOREIGN KEY columns and consider removing indexed views that reference several tables.
  • Force a plan with Query Store if the deadlock only occurs with a specific plan.
  • Access objects in the same order; split transactions; keep them short and with no user interaction; avoid hints (HOLDLOCK, SERIALIZABLE, READCOMMITTEDLOCK, REPEATABLEREAD, UPDLOCK, XLOCK, TABLOCK).
  • RCSI removes the S locks on reads; SNAPSHOT on reads if RCSI is OFF (with RCSI ON, deadlocks between writers can turn into update conflicts). Optimized locking in Azure SQL DB reduces deadlocks even further.
  • The application must always retry error 1205 with a random pause (see the concurrency patterns topic).
Exam: error 1205 = deadlock victim · 1222 = lock timeout · 3960 = snapshot update conflict. In Azure SQL DB the graph is captured with an XE session database_xml_deadlock_report (system_health belongs to SQL Server/MI) and you are notified with the Deadlocks signal.
Sources: Learn · Identify and resolve blocking and deadlocks · Docs · Analyze and prevent deadlocks in Azure SQL DB · Docs · Deadlocks guide · Docs · SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY
Module 7Domain 2 · 35–40%

Implement CI/CD by using SQL database projects

Declarative project (Microsoft.Build.Sql) → dotnet build → .dacpac → SqlPackage → environments with approvals. The exam tests the exact structure of the .sqlproj, the dotnet/sqlpackage commands, the GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps YAML, secrets/OIDC, schema drift, the testing strategy and the pipeline controls (branch policies, environments, CODEOWNERS).

Skills measured covered:
  • Design and implement a testing strategy, including unit tests and integration tests
  • Create and manage reference/static data in source control
  • Create, build, and validate database models by using SQL Database Projects, including SDK-style models
  • Configure source control for SQL Database Projects
  • Manage branching, pull requests, and conflict resolution
  • Implement secrets management
  • Detect schema drift by using SQL Database Projects
  • Update an SQL database project and deploy changes
  • Design and implement controls for deployment pipelines, including branching policies, triggers in approvals, authentication tables, and code owners

SQL database projects: SDK-style (Microsoft.Build.Sql) vs original (SSDT) SQL Server Azure SQL Fabric GA

A project stores the desired end state of each object in its own .sql (there are no sequential migration scripts). The build compiles it into a .dacpac and provides two things: validation (references between objects + syntax against the target platform) and a single artifact that travels through all environments (build once, deploy many). SqlPackage Publish computes the diff against the target: new DB → creates the objects in dependency order; existing DB → only the necessary ALTER statements (idempotent: the same .dacpac deployed 5 times changes nothing on the 5th).

Convert an original project to SDK-style (5 steps)

  1. Backup: MyProject.sqlproj → MyProject.sqlproj.original; build and save original_project.dacpac outside the project.
  2. Edit the .sqlproj: add <Sdk Name="Microsoft.Build.Sql" Version="#.#.#" /> inside <Project> and remove the <Import …> entries for SSDT targets, the Properties folder and the <Build Include="*.sql"> entries of the project folder.
  3. Do not remove: Build Include of .sql files outside the project tree, PreDeploy/PostDeploy, or non-.sql items (.publish.xml in None, .refactorlog in RefactorLog, .xsd).
  4. Solution (.sln): dotnet new sln + dotnet sln add …, or change the PROJECT_TYPE_GUID to 42EA0DBD-9CF1-443E-919E-BE9C484E4577.
  5. Build again and compare both .dacpac files with DacpacVerify (compares objects, pre/post scripts, SQLCMD variables, references and properties) or with Schema Compare (the latter only validates the model: no pre/post scripts, refactorlog or settings; DacpacVerify is recommended).
dotnet tool install --global Microsoft.DacpacVerify --prerelease
DacpacVerify original_project.dacpac modified_project.dacpac
Discrepancy: the module shows dotnet tool install -g microsoft.dacpacverify (no flag); the conversion guide in the documentation adds --prerelease. If the installation does not find a stable version, use the flag.

File structure and exact configuration of the .sqlproj (SDK-style) GA

In SDK-style the .sqlproj is minimal: SDK + properties + only the “special” items (pre/post, variables, references). The .sql files are not listed (globbing **/*.sql).

MyDatabaseProject/
├── MyDatabaseProject.sqlproj
├── .gitignore                    (bin/ obj/ *.dacpac *.user)
├── Tables/            Customers.sql, Orders.sql
├── Views/             vw_ActiveCustomers.sql
├── StoredProcedures/  usp_GetCustomerOrders.sql
├── Scripts/
│   ├── PreDeployment/   prep-db.sql
│   └── PostDeployment/  seed-statuses.sql, seed-regions.sql
└── PostDeploy.sql                (single post-deployment; uses :r to include Scripts/PostDeployment/*)
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Project DefaultTargets="Build">
  <Sdk Name="Microsoft.Build.Sql" Version="2.3.0" />
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Name>MyDatabaseProject</Name>
    <DSP>Microsoft.Data.Tools.Schema.Sql.Sql160DatabaseSchemaProvider</DSP>
    <ModelCollation>1033, CI</ModelCollation>
    <ProjectGuid>{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}</ProjectGuid>
    <RunSqlCodeAnalysis>True</RunSqlCodeAnalysis>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <PropertyGroup Condition="'$(Configuration)'=='Release'">
    <TreatTSqlWarningsAsErrors>True</TreatTSqlWarningsAsErrors>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PreDeploy Include="Scripts\PreDeployment\prep-db.sql" />
    <PostDeploy Include="PostDeploy.sql" />
    <Build Remove="Scripts\PostDeployment\seed-statuses.sql" />
    <None Include="Scripts\PostDeployment\seed-statuses.sql" />
    <SqlCmdVariable Include="EnvironmentName">
      <DefaultValue>testing</DefaultValue>
      <Value>$(SqlCmdVar__1)</Value>
    </SqlCmdVariable>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.SqlServer.Dacpacs.Master" Version="160.2.1" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
Form of the SDK reference: the official template (dotnet new sqlproj) and the documentation use the <Sdk Name="Microsoft.Build.Sql" Version="…" /> element inside <Project DefaultTargets="Build">. Version 2.3.0 (release notes: 2026-09-15) is the latest as of 2026-10-30; the template includes the placeholder ###ASSEMBLY_VERSION###, which is replaced by the current one. The docs, the template and the DacFx repo always use this <Sdk> element; they do not show the attribute form <Project Sdk="Microsoft.Build.Sql/x.y.z">.

Target platform (DSP), build and model validation GA

The .dacpac is the compiled model. The build checks every reference between objects and the syntax against the target platform: a view over a nonexistent column fails; a SQL Server 2025 vector function fails if the project targets Sql140. Full value: Microsoft.Data.Tools.Schema.Sql.<Suffix>DatabaseSchemaProvider.

Suffix (DSP)PlatformNote
Sql120 · Sql130 · Sql140 · Sql150SQL Server 2014 · 2016 · 2017 · 2019Sql120 is not offered in dotnet new -tp
Sql160SQL Server 2022The template labels it “2022/Azure SQL MI”
Sql170SQL Server 2025Template default; supported since Microsoft.Build.Sql 2.0.0
SqlAzureV12Azure SQL Database
SqlDbFabricSQL database in Fabric / Fabric mirrored SQL databaseLabeled preview in the target platform doc
SqlDw · SqlServerless · SqlDwUnifiedSynapse dedicated pool · Synapse serverless · Fabric Data Warehouse
 
dotnet new install Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates              # only once
dotnet new sqlproj -n MyDatabaseProject -tp SqlAzureV12 -g    # -tp platform · -g .gitignore
dotnet build MyDatabaseProject.sqlproj                        # → bin/Debug/MyDatabaseProject.dacpac
dotnet build -c Release -o ./output                           # → ./output/MyDatabaseProject.dacpac
dotnet build /p:DSP=Microsoft.Data.Tools.Schema.Sql.Sql150DatabaseSchemaProvider
  • Errors (block the build): broken reference, syntax not supported by the platform.
  • Warnings (do not block): inconsistent name casing and code analysis rules; TreatTSqlWarningsAsErrors or +!Rule turns them into errors.
  • The target platform travels in the .dacpac and is compared with the destination when publishing: if it does not match, the deploy exits before changing anything unless /p:AllowIncompatiblePlatform=true.

Code analysis (RunSqlCodeAnalysis): SR00xx rules in 3 categories — Design (SR0001 SELECT *, SR0008 SCOPE_IDENTITY instead of @@IDENTITY, SR0010 obsolete join syntax, SR0014 data loss in cast…), Naming (SR0011 special characters, SR0012 reserved words, SR0016 sp_ prefix) and Performance (SR0004 column without an index in IN, SR0005 LIKE '%…', SR0006, SR0007, SR0015). Suppress findings with StaticCodeAnalysis.SuppressMessages.xml (SuppressedFile + SuppressedRule Category="Microsoft.Rules.Data" RuleId="SR0001").

Inspect and start from an existing DB

  • Inspect the artifact: rename .dacpac → .zip and extract; there is a single .sql for each pre/post script with the combined T-SQL of all the :r includes.
  • Project from a DB: Schema Compare (DB → empty project) or sqlpackage /Action:Extract … /p:ExtractTarget=SqlProject (generates .sqlproj + one .sql per object).
  • Only the .sql files: /p:ExtractTarget=SchemaObjectType (folders by schema and type) and create the .sqlproj with the template.
Watch out: dotnet new sqlproj needs the template installed (dotnet new install Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates; the module does not mention it) and by default targets Sql170. For Azure SQL Database use -tp SqlAzureV12; if the destination does not match, the publish stops.
Exam: “the build fails because a function does not exist in the version” → the DSP is older than the function. “Warnings that do not break the build” → TreatTSqlWarningsAsErrors is False (default).
Sources: Learn · Create, build, and validate SQL database projects · Docs · Target platform · Docs · SQL code analysis · Docs · Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates

SqlPackage: actions and parameters (Publish, Script, DeployReport, DriftReport, Extract, Export, Import) GA

Cross-platform CLI on top of DacFx: SqlPackage /Action:<Action> {parameters} {/p:properties} {/v:SQLCMD variables}. In CI install it as a dotnet tool (requires .NET SDK; tool for .NET 8+): dotnet tool install --global Microsoft.SqlPackage; update with dotnet tool update -g microsoft.sqlpackage; pin the version with --version; previews with --prerelease; check with SqlPackage /Version. Version as of 2026-10-30: 170.5.96.

ActionWhat it doesInput → output
PublishIncrementally updates the target schema to match the .dacpac; creates the DB if it does not exist/SourceFile → /TargetConnectionString; optional /DeployScriptPath, /DeployReportPath
ScriptGenerates the incremental T-SQL without running itsame → /DeployScriptPath or /OutputPath (both valid in Script; Learn uses /OutputPath in unit 2 and /DeployScriptPath in unit 5)
DeployReportXML with what Publish would do (Create, Alter, Drop, TableDataMotion)same → /OutputPath (the docs also use /DeployReportPath)
DriftReportXML with the changes made to a registered DB since it was registeredonly /TargetConnectionString → /OutputPath
ExtractReverse engineering of the DB into a .dacpac or into a project/files/SourceConnectionString → /TargetFile; /p:ExtractTarget= DacPac (default) | SqlProject | SchemaObjectType | Schema | ObjectType | Flat | File
Export / ImportDB → .bacpac (schema and data) / .bacpac → new DBportability and archiving

/TargetFile:/tf:Extract/Export output

/DeployScriptPath: · /DeployReportPath: · /OutputPath:/dsp: · /drp: · /op:Script/report during Publish or Script · output of DeployReport, DriftReport and Script
